intro: Three of these six stand in one small park in downtown Hilo, two more are a short walk away, and the sixth marks a shoreline named for coconuts before anyone registered one. Hawaii protects individual trees by law rather than the ground they stand on. Kalakaua Park holds a banyan planted in 1882, a Caribbean divi-divi, and an endangered native palm. A tropical almond of about 206 years stands outside a church on Haili Street, and a coconut palm on the Waiolama Canal recalls a grove an 1864 chant already sang about.
meta_description: Six protected trees in Hilo: an 1882 banyan, a Caribbean divi-divi, an endangered native palm, and a coconut shoreline sung about in 1864.
question_meta: Hilo's oldest tree is the kamani outside Haili Congregational Church, about 206 years. Its story, and the other protected trees around town.
question_answer:
The oldest tree in Hilo is the kamani at the corner of Haili Street and Ululani Street, on the pavement outside Haili Congregational Church. The Hawaii Tribune-Herald put its age at 194 years in 2014, which makes it about 206 now, so it was standing here before the church beside it and before Hilo was a town of any size. Hawaii's exceptional-tree register records it at 12.2 metres round and rates its condition good.

One caution about its name, because the register and the town disagree. The register files it as a False Kamani, Terminalia catappa, the tropical almond. Local usage, including that newspaper piece, drops the qualifier and calls it a kamani, which botanically means a different tree altogether, Calophyllum inophyllum. This page follows the register on the species and the newspaper on the age.

What makes it visible from across the street: Terminalia catappa throws its branches out in flat horizontal whorls that stack up the trunk, so it reads as a series of green plates rather than a dome, and its leaves turn red and drop in a place where almost nothing else changes colour.
question_context:
Hawaii protects trees in an unusual way and it shapes this whole page. Act 105 of 1975 lets each county designate individual specimens as exceptional trees, and the designation attaches to the tree rather than to the land, which is why the register names single trunks in car parks and on street corners instead of naming woodland. The City and County of Honolulu publishes the resulting database under a public-domain dedication, and despite its title it covers all four counties.

Two things about that source govern what this page can say. It carries no age field at all, so every year given here comes from a newspaper or a local history rather than from the register, and where nobody has published one the page says so instead of estimating. And its coordinates are rounded to about a kilometre, with several Kalakaua Park trees sharing a single point between them, so every pin here is marked approximate and each entry describes what to look for once you are standing in the right park. See the full list of six on the Hilo page.

faq.q: What is the oldest tree in Hilo?
faq.a: The kamani outside Haili Congregational Church, at the corner of Haili and Ululani Streets. A 2014 newspaper piece put it at 194 years, which makes it about 206 now. The register records 12.2 metres of girth and rates its condition good.

faq.q: Can I see them all in one walk?
faq.a: Mostly. Three of the six share Kalakaua Park in the middle of downtown, the kamani is a few minutes away on Haili Street, the coconut palm is a short walk from downtown along the Waiolama Canal, and the sixth is in Wailuku River State Park at Rainbow Falls, about two kilometres out and worth the detour for the falls as much as the tree.

Yes, all six. Kalakaua Park is a public square open daily, the kamani stands on a public pavement, the coconut palm is inside the free Wailoa River State Recreation Area, and Wailuku River State Park is free and open from sunrise to sunset.

faq.q: Why are the pins marked approximate?
faq.a: Because the register's coordinates are rounded to roughly a kilometre and several trees in Kalakaua Park share one point between them. Marking a pin confirmed on that basis would be inventing a precision nobody has, so each entry describes what to look for instead.

trees.name: The Kalakaua Park Banyan
trees.story:
Two men are credited with planting this banyan and they cannot both be right. Wikipedia and a Hilo guide both say Sheriff Luther Severance put it in at the west end of Kalakaua Park in 1882, which makes it about 144 years old. A newspaper account from 1964 credits King Kalakaua himself. Neither source settles it and this page does not pick.

What is not in dispute is the size. The exceptional-tree register puts 18.6 metres around it, and that figure is not a trunk: Ficus benghalensis drops aerial roots that thicken into props, and the measurement runs around the whole buttressed mass. Standing under one is less like meeting a tree than walking into a room with a ceiling.

It had a twin. When Waianuenue Avenue was widened, Sheriff George Williams had the other original moved about five miles up to Kaumana, which in 1882 terms is a remarkable thing to attempt and in any terms is a remarkable thing to survive.

Hawaii protects individual trees by law, under Act 105 of 1975, and the designation attaches to the specimen rather than to the ground it stands on. This one is in the middle of downtown Hilo with a lawn under it and two more protected trees in the same small park.
trees.transport: No dedicated stop; central downtown Hilo, an easy walk from the bayfront and most Hilo accommodation
trees.how_to_recognise: The huge banyan at the west end of Kalakaua Park, with aerial roots come down as props. Impossible to miss and impossible to mistake for the park's other two protected trees.

trees.name: The Haili Street Kamani

location.address: Corner of Haili Street and Ululani Street, Hilo, outside Haili Congregational Church

trees.story:
The register calls it a False Kamani and the newspaper that loves it does not. In 2014 the Hawaii Tribune-Herald ran a piece on the treasured kamani tree at the corner of Haili and Ululani, gave its age as 194 years, and left the qualifier off, which is the usual local shorthand. Botanically the two are unrelated: true kamani is Calophyllum inophyllum, and this is Terminalia catappa, the tropical almond, whose leaves turn red and drop in a place where almost nothing else changes colour.

Take the newspaper's figure forward and the tree is about 206 years old now, which puts it here before the church it stands beside, before Hilo was a town of any size, and before anyone thought to write down what was growing on this corner.

The register records 12.2 metres around it and rates its condition good. Terminalia catappa grows in tiers, with branches thrown out in flat horizontal whorls that stack up the trunk, so from across the street it reads as a series of green plates rather than a dome.

It stands on the pavement outside Haili Congregational Church, which means you can walk up to it at any hour without asking anyone.
trees.access: Free, on a public street corner outside Haili Congregational Church
trees.transport: No dedicated stop; downtown Hilo, an easy walk from Kalakaua Park and the bayfront
trees.how_to_recognise: On the pavement at the corner of Haili and Ululani, outside Haili Congregational Church. Branches in flat stacked tiers rather than a rounded crown.

location_site.name: Haili Congregational Church, corner of Haili and Ululani Streets

trees.name: The Rainbow Falls Banyan

location.address: Wailuku River State Park (Rainbow Falls), along the trail beyond the upper viewing platform, Hilo

trees.story:
The register designates this tree and then records nothing about it. No girth, no height, no condition: just an Indian banyan at Rainbow Falls, protected under Act 105 like the rest, with every measurement column left blank.

So what stands here is described rather than measured. It grows along the trail that continues past the upper viewing platform above the falls, away from the crowd that stops at the railing, and it is the sprawling aerial-root kind of banyan rather than a single trunk: props coming down from the limbs and rooting where they land, which is how one of these walks slowly sideways over a century.

Nobody has published an age for it either, and that is the honest state of it rather than a gap we intend to fill with arithmetic. Banyans cannot be aged from girth anyway, because the figure would be a measurement of the whole colony rather than of one stem.

Wailuku River State Park is open daily from early morning to late afternoon, free for Hawaii residents and a small fee for visitors, and the falls themselves are the reason most people come. The tree is the thing you find by walking two minutes further than they do. If you know when it went in, tell us.
trees.access: Wailuku River State Park (Rainbow Falls) is open daily 7:00am to 5:30pm, gates lock at 6:00pm. Entry is free for Hawaii residents with ID; non-residents pay $5 (children 3 and under free) plus $10 per vehicle for parking, card only, one fee also covers Boiling Pots. Fees required since January 2026.
trees.transport: A short drive or taxi ride from downtown Hilo; the tree stands past the upper viewing platform along the park trail, an easy walk from the parking area.
trees.how_to_recognise: Keep walking past the upper viewing platform above the falls. The sprawling banyan with props rooting into the ground, not the falls themselves.

trees.name: The Divi-Divi of Kalakaua Park
trees.story:
A divi-divi is a strange thing to find protected in a Hawaiian town square. Caesalpinia coriaria comes from the dry forests of the Caribbean and Central America, it is the national tree of Curacao, and its seed pods were harvested for the tannin that turned hides into leather. Nothing about that story runs through Hilo, which gets more than three metres of rain a year.

It is here anyway, at 3.3 metres round, in good condition, one of three protected trees in Kalakaua Park along with the 1882 banyan and an endangered native palm. Hilo's own downtown walking tour includes the park's trees and describes them as more than a century old as a group, which is corroboration for the park and not a date for this tree, so no age is claimed here.

The species is worth looking at properly once you find it. Divi-divi grow slowly and hold their branches in a lopsided, wind-combed way even where there is no wind, and the pods curl into tight brown spirals that look more like something that fell off an animal than off a tree.

The park is small, open daily and free, and it sits in the middle of downtown, which makes all three of its trees one short stop rather than three.
trees.transport: No dedicated stop; central downtown Hilo, an easy walk from the bayfront and most Hilo accommodation
trees.how_to_recognise: The smallest of the three protected trees in Kalakaua Park, with lopsided wind-combed branches and tightly curled brown seed pods.

trees.name: The Loulu Palm of Kalakaua Park
trees.story:
This palm is endangered in the wild and it is growing in a public park. Pritchardia beccariana is one of roughly two dozen loulu species found nowhere on earth but Hawaii, all of them threatened, and this one is native to the Big Island specifically. Rats eat the seeds, which is most of why they are disappearing.

Hawaii's exceptional-tree register lists it at 26 feet tall and rates its condition fair, which is an honest reading rather than a reassuring one. No girth is recorded, and none would help: a palm is not a tree in the way the ageing arithmetic assumes, with no annual rings and no secondary thickening, so nobody can put a number on how long it has stood here.

Loulu once covered lowland Hawaii in forests dense enough that early accounts describe them as impassable. What is left is scattered specimens and small protected stands, which makes a healthy one in the middle of Hilo something closer to a museum piece than a park planting.

It shares Kalakaua Park with the banyan and the divi-divi, so all three are one stop, and it is the only one of them that belongs here.
trees.transport: No dedicated stop; central downtown Hilo, an easy walk from the bayfront and most Hilo accommodation
trees.how_to_recognise: A fan palm in Kalakaua Park, not one of the feather-leaved coconuts. It is the only palm among the park's three protected trees.

trees.name: The Coconut of Waiolama Canal

location.address: Wailoa River State Recreation Area, along the Waiolama Canal near Pauahi Street, Hilo

trees.story:
This shoreline was named for coconuts a century before anyone thought to register one. Waiolama's older name is Waiolama Niu, niu meaning coconut, and an 1864 chant already sings of the coconut grove of Piʻopiʻo standing on these banks, now inside the Wailoa River State Recreation Area. A local history of the area describes the mid-1800s shore as luxuriant with coconut trees, so whichever specimen the state's exceptional-tree register singles out today stands where a much older grove once did.

It has survived worse than time passing. Hilo's tsunamis of 1946 and 1960 tore through this exact stretch of shoreline, and local accounts credit the coconut, banyan and mango trees along the canal with saving lives, people caught in the wave climbing into their limbs and holding on until the water dropped. The register lists this palm's condition as good and its owner as the State of Hawaii, inside what is now a 132-acre park.

Nobody has measured its girth or dated it, and a coconut palm would not tell you either way, it carries no growth rings. The register also does not say exactly which trunk along the canal it designated, so look for a mature, substantial palm near the water rather than a marked one, and if you know which it is, tell us.
trees.access: Free, within Wailoa River State Recreation Area (Division of State Parks), open daily during daylight hours, no entrance fee, no check-in required
trees.transport: A short walk from downtown Hilo; the recreation area borders Kamehameha Avenue and Pauahi Street, a few minutes from Kalakaua Park
trees.how_to_recognise: Along the Waiolama Canal in Wailoa River State Recreation Area, near Pauahi Street; look for a mature palm near the water, since the register does not pin the exact trunk.

trees.name: The Babe Ruth Banyan of Banyan Drive

location.address: In front of the Hilo Hawaiian Hotel, 71 Banyan Drive, Hilo, HI 96720

trees.access: Free. Banyan Drive is a public road with a shoreline walk; the tree stands at the road edge by the Hilo Hawaiian Hotel frontage, state land looked after by the county and the hotel lessees.
trees.transport: Hele-On buses serve downtown Hilo; Banyan Drive is about 1.5 km (20 minutes on foot) from Kalakaua Park, or 5 minutes by car.
trees.how_to_recognise: You can recognise it by its brown wooden plaque naming Babe Ruth, if the plaque survives; many have rotted or gone. Keola Magazine places it on the Banyan Drive frontage of the Hilo Hawaiian Hotel.
facts: Planted 28 October 1933, Babe Ruth's first day in Hilo for an exhibition game; one week after Cecil B. DeMille's tree (20 Oct 1933). Keola Magazine: https://keolamagazine.com/sustainability/hilos-history-through-the-banyan-trees/
Keola says the tree still stands in front of what is now the Hilo Hawaiian Hotel. Another source (travel summary) placed it at Grand Naniloa; Keola names the Hilo Hawaiian.
About 50 of the celebrity banyans remain along the drive, marked by plaques (Wikipedia, Garden Design, Keola).

Banyan Drive trees are threatened by an invasive gall wasp and one on the east side partially collapsed in 2022 (Big Island Now): https://bigislandnow.com/2022/11/19/majestic-banyan-collapses-along-iconic-hilo-road-highlighting-need-for-tree-saving-plan/
Planting date 1933 for Ruth also in Garden Design photo caption and Wikipedia text.
trees.verify_notes: Alive: Keola Magazine (undated, recent; says it still stands); Civil Beat 2025-07 says trees along the drive bear plaques and are struggling, but names no loss of Ruth's tree. Position is the hotel frontage point from OSM/Nominatim (way 248966840), approximate: no source pins the individual trunk and exact plaque side is not known. One source says Grand Naniloa; Keola and the Hilo Hawaiian frontage claim agree with the Wikipedia/Keola chain, but this is a conflict to flag. Age basis is a documented planting date for this specimen; ages 90 to 93 years in 2026. No girth or height published. No private land: public drive. Not a walk-through ensemble; one named tree with a plaque. Flagged: one-source on location (Keola), pin approximate.
trees.story:
Babe Ruth planted this banyan on 28 October 1933, his first day in Hilo, where he had come to play an exhibition game. Cecil B. DeMille had planted his own a week earlier, on 20 October, and both trees belong to the celebrity plantings that line Banyan Drive.

About fifty of those celebrity banyans still line the drive, each once marked with a brown wooden plaque naming its planter. Keola Magazine, which traced their history, says Ruth's still stands in front of what is now the Hilo Hawaiian Hotel. One travel summary puts it at the Grand Naniloa instead, so if the plaque you find disagrees with this page, the plaque wins and we would like to hear about it.

That plaque is the way to find it, and it may not be there. Keola reports that many of the signs have rotted or gone missing, and the trees themselves are under strain. An invasive gall wasp has been at work along the drive, and in 2022 Big Island Now reported one banyan on the east side partially collapsing. A 2025 piece in Civil Beat described the drive's trees as struggling. Nobody has reported losing Ruth's.

It is about 93 years old, dated by the day it went in. Nobody has published its girth or height, and a photograph of the tree with its plaque would help us more than anything.

trees.name: The Amelia Earhart Banyan

location.address: Banyan Drive, Waiakea Peninsula, Hilo, HI 96720 (exact side of the loop not published)

trees.access: Free. Banyan Drive is a public road with a shoreline walk.
trees.transport: Hele-On buses serve downtown Hilo; Banyan Drive is about 1.5 km from Kalakaua Park, or 5 minutes by car.
trees.how_to_recognise: You can recognise it only by its plaque, a brown wooden sign naming Amelia Earhart; some plaques along the drive are rotted or missing. It stands somewhere on the Banyan Drive loop, side not published.
facts: Planted in 1935, five days before Earhart's Honolulu to Oakland solo flight (Keola, Garden Design 'several days before'; Wikipedia gallery caption 1935).

Civil Beat opinion 2025-07: Earhart planted one of the plaqued banyans; the drive's trees are wilting in neglect, insects in the bark. https://www.civilbeat.org/2025/07/will-bailey-collapse-of-banyan-drive-is-a-sign-of-hilos-selective-neglect/
Wikipedia also lists Earhart with Knefler McGinnis and Lincoln Ellsworth among adventurer planters.
Commons file 'Banyan Drive, Hilo - Amelia Earhart.jpg' (photo dated 2020-03-09, description 'Planted by Amelia Earhart') shows the plaqued tree standing in 2020.
trees.verify_notes: Alive: Commons photo 2020-03-09, Keola (recent undated), Civil Beat July 2025 names her tree among the plaqued banyans, none reported lost. WEAK ON PIN: no source places her tree on the loop; the coordinate is a point on Banyan Drive, NOT the tree. Findable only through the plaque; the writer must say the plaques are the way to find it and that some are missing (Keola). Planting-day detail (6 January 1935) appears only in a search summary, not fetched, so not recorded as fact. Recommend shipping only if the 'find the plaque' recognition line is acceptable; otherwise lead.
trees.story:
Amelia Earhart planted a banyan in Hilo in 1935, a few days before she flew solo from Honolulu to Oakland. Keola Magazine puts the gap at five days, Garden Design at several, and both put the tree first and the Pacific second.

It is one of roughly fifty plaqued banyans along Banyan Drive, and Wikipedia's account of the drive files her with the other adventurers who planted there, Knefler McGinnis and Lincoln Ellsworth among them. The evidence says it is still standing. A photograph on Wikimedia Commons dated March 2020 shows the plaqued tree standing, and a July 2025 opinion piece in Civil Beat named her tree among them while warning that the drive's trees were wilting from neglect, with insects in the bark.

Here is the honest part. No source we have read says where on the loop her tree stands, and the pin on this page marks Banyan Drive, not the trunk. The only reliable way to find it is to walk the drive and read the plaques, and Keola reports that many of those brown wooden signs have rotted or gone missing. Allow time, and treat it as a walk past fifty trees with one name to find.

It is about 91 years old, dated by her visit. If you find the plaque, send us a photograph and the spot, and the pin moves to the tree.

trees.name: The Roosevelt Banyan of Banyan Drive

location.address: Banyan Drive, Waiakea Peninsula, Hilo, HI 96720 (exact side of the loop not published)

trees.access: Free. Banyan Drive is a public road with a shoreline walk.
trees.transport: Hele-On buses serve downtown Hilo; Banyan Drive is about 1.5 km from Kalakaua Park, or 5 minutes by car.
trees.how_to_recognise: You can recognise it by its brown wooden plaque naming President Franklin D. Roosevelt; some plaques on the drive have rotted or gone. It stands somewhere on the Banyan Drive loop, side not published.
facts: FDR arrived in Hilo on 25 July 1934 aboard the USS Houston for five hours; crews cleared brush and laid a crushed-coral road for him. He did not leave his car: he touched the tree and threw dirt on its base from the car (Jane Hoff in Keola). https://keolamagazine.com/sustainability/hilos-history-through-the-banyan-trees/

Civil Beat opinion July 2025: one banyan on the drive carries Roosevelt's name, from when Hilo smoothed the road for his 1934 motorcade. https://www.civilbeat.org/2025/07/will-bailey-collapse-of-banyan-drive-is-a-sign-of-hilos-selective-neglect/
Wikipedia: the drive was built in 1934 on the news of FDR's visit; about 50 plaqued banyans remain.
trees.verify_notes: Alive: Civil Beat July 2025 names the Roosevelt tree among the plaqued banyans, none reported lost; Big Island Now 2022 reports one east-side banyan partially collapsed (not identified as FDR's) and gall-wasp damage. PIN IS THE STREET, NOT THE TREE: no source places the Roosevelt tree; point is on Banyan Drive. Keola says it is touched, not planted, by FDR, so say 'the tree he touched'. Same findability caveat as hbi_008. Age is the documented 1934 planting; 92 years in 2026.
trees.story:
Franklin D. Roosevelt never got out of the car. On 25 July 1934 he came ashore at Hilo from the USS Houston for a visit of five hours, and according to the account in Keola Magazine he touched this banyan and threw dirt on its base from where he sat. So this is less the tree a president planted than the tree a president touched.

The town had gone to some trouble. Crews cleared brush and laid a crushed-coral road for the motorcade, and Wikipedia's history of Banyan Drive says the road itself was built in 1934 on the news that he was coming. A Civil Beat opinion piece in July 2025 makes the same link, tying the banyan that carries his name to the day Hilo smoothed the road for his motorcade.

That makes it about 92 years old, dated by the visit, and one of roughly fifty plaqued banyans still on the drive. They are not all in good shape. Big Island Now reported in 2022 that an invasive gall wasp was damaging the trees and that one on the east side had partially collapsed, though not, as far as anyone has said, this one.

No published source says where on the loop it stands, and the pin marks the road rather than the trunk. Look for a brown wooden plaque with his name, and know that some of the plaques have rotted or disappeared. If you find it, send us the spot.
